text: The Taliban has released a biography of leader Mullah Mohammed Omar, aimed at dispelling rumors of his death and reasserting his authority. The 11-page document, released on the Taliban's website, provides details on Omar's life and daily routine, and seeks to remind the world of his jihadi leadership credentials. The biography comes at a time when the Taliban faces a leadership crisis and rival militant groups, including ISIS, seek to gain influence.

Hundreds attended the funeral of Walter Scott, a black man shot and killed by a white police officer in South Carolina. The service was a celebration of Scott's life and a call for change, with speakers condemning racism and police brutality. Scott's family and supporters said his death could be a catalyst for change in America.

Former TSA agent Daniel Boykin sentenced to 6 months in jail for secretly videotaping female co-worker in bathroom. Over 90 videos and 1,500 photos of victim found on his devices. Boykin also pleaded guilty to aggravated burglary and computer violations.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage to boost its economy, which lacks conventional natural resources. The country is hosting events like the Kriol Jazz Festival and the Atlantic Music Expo to promote its music and attract tourists. Music could become a key sector for economic growth, with tourism expected to account for 20% of GDP by 2024.

Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 to keep their Premier League title hopes alive, staying within four points of leader Chelsea. The win, courtesy of Aaron Ramsey's first-half goal, keeps Arsenal in second place. The two teams will meet next week in a potentially title-deciding match.

The original cast of Twin Peaks, including Sherilyn Fenn and Sheryl Lee, have released a video supporting creator David Lynch in his salary dispute with Showtime. Lynch exited the project on Sunday, citing a lack of sufficient funding. The network hopes to still produce the revival with another creator.

Andrew Getty, 47, grandson of oil tycoon J. Paul Getty, died of natural causes, police said. The Los Angeles Police Department found no evidence of foul play and an autopsy is scheduled. Getty had filed for a restraining order against an ex-girlfriend recently, citing a serious medical condition.

Maryland police have taken Nyia Parler, 41, into custody to face charges in Philadelphia for allegedly abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in woods for over four days. Parler cannot be extradited until she completes unspecified "treatment" for a reason that is not being disclosed due to federal health care privacy laws. If extradited, she will face charges including aggravated assault and recklessly endangering another person.

Malala Yousafzai, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning education activist, has been honored with an asteroid named after her. The asteroid, discovered in 2010, was renamed 316201 Malala by NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer. The asteroid orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter.

About 100 people on the cruise ship Celebrity Infinity have fallen ill with gastrointestinal symptoms, including vomiting and diarrhea. The cause of the outbreak is still unknown. Two CDC staffers will board the ship in San Diego on Monday to investigate.

Here is a 2-3 sentence summary of the article:

The "Star Wars" saga is now available on digital HD, just in time for fans to binge-watch ahead of new releases. Mindy Kaling's brother has revealed that he posed as a black man to get into medical school, sparking controversy. Other trending stories include the death of "Dukes of Hazzard" actor James Best and a couple who got a free wedding from Burger King.

A Philadelphia woman, Keonna Thomas, 30, has been charged with trying to travel to join ISIS. Thomas is one of three women arrested this week on terror charges, with two New York women also taken into custody. The arrests highlight the growing threat of decentralized terrorist plots.

HBO releases teaser video for season 2 of "True Detective", premiering June 21. The new season stars Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams, and Taylor Kitsch in a story of conspiracy and betrayal in California. The plot follows a bizarre murder that brings together law enforcement and a career criminal.

Massachusetts authorities have charged 32-year-old Carlos Colina with assault and improper disposal of a body after human remains were found in a duffel bag in Cambridge over the weekend. The remains were identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, who knew Colina. Additional charges may be pending as police continue to analyze evidence.

Trey Moses, a top college basketball recruit, asked Ellie Meredith, a high school freshman with Down syndrome, to be his prom date. The surprise invitation, made in front of Ellie's classmates, has gone viral on social media. Ellie's parents and Trey's coaches and family members have praised his kind gesture.

NBC debuts "A.D. The Bible Continues," a sequel to the History Channel hit, this Sunday. The miniseries follows Jesus' resurrection and early Christianity. Other notable shows premiering or returning this week include "Mad Men," "American Odyssey," "Louie," "The Comedians," and "Marvel's Daredevil."

Indiana Governor Mike Pence signed a religious freedom law critics say allows discrimination against gays and lesbians. The move has sparked backlash and highlighted divisions within the Republican Party on social issues. The controversy may push the party further right ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

Apple has released a new version of its mobile operating system with more diverse emojis, including a range of skin tones, same-sex couples, and a rainbow flag. The update allows users to choose skin tones for each human emoji, including Santa Claus. The new emojis have been met with both praise and criticism, with some conservatives expressing outrage over the inclusion of gay couples.

Singer Avril Lavigne reveals she was bedridden for five months with Lyme disease, which she contracted from a tick bite. The 30-year-old Canadian musician says she was initially undiagnosed and at one point thought she was dying. Lavigne is now 80 percent better and releasing a new single.

New research suggests Anne Frank and her sister Margot died at least a month earlier than previously thought, likely in February 1945, due to complications from typhus. The sisters were prisoners at the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, where they were exposed to the disease and suffered in inhumane conditions. The exact dates of their deaths remain unclear.

Two Troy University students, Ryan Calhoun and Delonte Martistee, have been arrested and charged with gang raping a woman on spring break in Panama City Beach, Florida. The alleged rape was captured on video and took place behind a popular bar and dance club between March 10-12, 2015. The investigation is ongoing with more arrests expected.

A stray dog in Washington State was hit by a car, apparently killed with a hammer, and buried, but miraculously survived and was found days later. The dog, now named Theia, is receiving treatment at a veterinary hospital and has raised over $10,000 in donations to cover her care. Despite her ordeal, Theia is described as gentle and loving, and is expected to make a full recovery with further surgery and care.

FBI confirms that Zulkifli bin Hir, aka Marwan, a Malaysian bomb maker and one of its most wanted terrorists, was killed in a January raid in the Philippines. The operation, which aimed to capture Marwan, resulted in the deaths of 44 Philippine police commandos and damaged peace efforts with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. The FBI had offered a $5 million reward for information leading to Marwan's capture.

US President Barack Obama's nuclear deal with Iran has been criticized for giving up too much leverage, allowing Tehran to keep its nuclear infrastructure and receive billions of dollars in sanctions relief. Critics argue that the deal does not impose tough enough safeguards to prevent Iran from cheating and that it fails to address the country's support for terrorist groups. The deal's critics are calling for stricter sanctions and more robust verification mechanisms.

The final season of "Mad Men" premieres Sunday, marking the end of an era for the hit AMC series. The show, which has become a cultural phenomenon, follows the characters as they navigate the changing times of the late 1960s. The new season is expected to tackle major events, including the moon landing, and may see the departure of several longtime characters.

A giraffe named Katie gave birth to a baby at the Dallas Zoo, with the birth streamed live on Animal Planet's website. The newborn, estimated to be 6 feet tall, appeared to be healthy, moving its ears and attempting to stand and nurse. The zoo has not released the baby's gender or further details.

US Attorney General nominee Loretta Lynch's confirmation is delayed, with some supporters attributing the delay to racial bias. Lynch, the first African-American woman nominated for the position, cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in February but a full Senate vote has not been scheduled. Her supporters are organizing to pressure Republican Senators to support her confirmation.

Gunmen stormed the attorney general's office in northern Afghanistan, killing three people and wounding five others. Afghan security forces exchanged fire with the assailants, with efforts to rescue staff and civilians ongoing. The incident is still unfolding.

Bob Barker, the former host of "The Price Is Right", made a surprise return to the show on April 1, hosting the first game in eight years. Barker, 91, led the show's "Lucky Seven" segment before handing over to current host Drew Carey. It was Barker's first appearance on the show since stepping down as host in 2007.

Blues legend B.B. King was hospitalized for dehydration caused by his Type II diabetes, but has been released and is recovering at home. The 89-year-old musician, also known as the "King of the Blues," is feeling better after expressing gratitude for concerns about his health. King is a 15-time Grammy winner with hits like "The Thrill Is Gone" and "When Love Comes to Town."

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing. The verdict raises questions about preventing similar violence, with some arguing that radicalization is driven by politics, religion, and identity. Experts say that rather than reforming Islam, understanding and addressing grievances and promoting community engagement can help counter extremism.

Videos of the week include a tour of Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion, a thrilling ride on the world's tallest and fastest "giga-coaster", and a CNN exclusive interview with a former student of Bikram yoga creator Bikram Choudhury, who alleges he sexually assaulted her. Other videos feature eyewitness accounts of the Germanwings plane crash and discussions on the Indiana religious freedom law. Several viral videos also explore science and pop culture.

The Pentagon released a map showing coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of Iraqi territory seized by ISIS. The gains are largely in central and northern areas, but a counterinsurgency expert says it's too early to say the tide is turning. ISIS is adapting to losses by launching asymmetric attacks elsewhere, experts say.

A passenger on an Air Canada flight from Toronto to Atlanta tried to choke another passenger with a cord, reportedly telling others he was there to kill him. The suspect was subdued by other passengers and escorted off the plane by US authorities after landing. The incident is under investigation, with the suspect taken for a mental evaluation.

Hong Kong police found two dead women, one on the floor with neck and buttock cuts and the other in a suitcase on the balcony, after responding to a call at a Wan Chai apartment. Rurik Jutting, a 29-year-old former banker, was charged with two counts of murder; a court hearing was adjourned until May. The victims, identified as Sumarti Ningsih and Seneng Mujiasih, were Indonesian domestic workers who had worked in Hong Kong.

Multiple tornadoes ripped through the rural Midwest on Thursday, with one massive twister tearing through Rochelle, Illinois, and another touching down in Iowa and Missouri. At least one person died in Illinois, and dozens of homes were damaged or destroyed across several states. The storms caused widespread destruction but relatively few casualties.

Don McLean's manuscript of "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at a Christie's auction. The 1971 song has been the subject of much speculation and analysis over its lyrics and meaning. The sale ranks as the third highest auction price for an American literary manuscript.

UNRWA Commissioner-General Pierre Krähenbühl will make an emergency visit to the Yarmouk Palestinian refugee camp in Syria to assess the humanitarian situation. The camp, home to 18,000 Palestinians and Syrian civilians, has been under fire since 2012 and cut off from aid since 2013. Krähenbühl will meet with Syrian officials and displaced people to address the crisis.

Hundreds have been killed and tens of thousands displaced in Yemen as Saudi-led coalition airstrikes target Houthi rebels, with the conflict threatening to worsen a humanitarian crisis. The airstrikes have destroyed infrastructure, leaving millions without electricity and at risk of losing access to clean water. The International Committee of the Red Cross has called for a humanitarian ceasefire to allow aid to reach civilians.

Richie Benaud, the former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster, has died at the age of 84. Benaud was a record-breaking leg-spinner and captain who became cricket's most famous and iconic commentator. He was inducted into the Sport Australia Hall of Fame in 1985 and commentated on cricket for over four decades with the BBC.

A total lunar eclipse, lasting nearly 5 minutes, is visible in western North America and parts of Asia and South America. The eclipse, which began at 3:16 a.m. PDT, is the shortest of the century, lasting 4 minutes and 43 seconds. A partial eclipse is visible across the US, but sunrise will interrupt viewing on the East Coast.

Robert Durst, a 71-year-old millionaire real estate heir, has been charged with unlawful possession of a firearm, a federal grand jury indictment alleges. Durst, a convicted felon, faces up to 10 years in prison if found guilty. He also faces first-degree murder charges in connection with the 2000 killing of Susan Berman.

Paul Walker, star of the "Fast and Furious" franchise, is remembered by fans and colleagues on the release of "Furious 7", the film he was filming when he died in a car crash in 2013. The film's release has sparked tributes and emotional reactions, with co-star Vin Diesel calling it "more than a movie". Walker's character was completed using special effects and body doubles after his death.

On "The Price Is Right", model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed the prize for a contestant, a new Hyundai Sonata. Host Drew Carey burst out laughing as Arbelaez attempted to hide. The incident occurred during a chaotic week for the show.

Thai Smile, a subsidiary of Thai Airways, has unveiled an Airbus A320 with a colorful "Adventure Time" livery featuring characters from the Cartoon Network show. The plane's interior is also themed around the show, with character designs on overhead bins and air sickness bags. The special plane will make its inaugural flight from Bangkok to Phuket on April 4.

A brood of baby ducks and their mother caused a commotion on a Washington street, crossing a heavily trafficked road with the help of pedestrians. The pedestrians stopped traffic and guided the ducks to a safer area, with one man giving up his umbrella to help corral the ducklings. The incident was captured by CNN correspondents who were on the scene.

French investigators have finished collecting evidence from the crash site of Germanwings Flight 9525, which killed 150 people on March 24. The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been found, and DNA profiles have been isolated from samples collected at the site. Authorities believe co-pilot Andreas Lubitz intentionally crashed the plane after locking out the captain.

Cuba and the US are set to discuss re-establishing formal relations and re-opening embassies after a decades-long rift. The two nations' leaders may interact at a regional summit in Panama, despite a brawl between Cuban government supporters and anti-Castro protesters. A US decision to remove Cuba from a list of state sponsors of terrorism could pave the way for improved ties.

Jesus and his disciples likely supported themselves through donations from supporters, including wealthy women such as Mary Magdalene and Joanna, who provided for them out of their resources. The Jesus community also had a common purse and may have relied on begging and hospitality to meet their basic needs. Some scholars believe that Jesus' ministry received substantial donations from affluent backers, including men like Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus.

California regulator orders Pacific Gas & Electric Co. to pay $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe operation of its gas transmission system, including 2010 pipeline rupture that killed 8. Most of penalty is in forced spending on pipeline safety improvements. The fine is a record for the state.

Lauren Hill, a 19-year-old college basketball player who inspired millions with her courageous fight against brain cancer, has died. Hill's story went viral last year when she played in her first collegiate game after the NCAA moved up her team's schedule to accommodate her. She had raised $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research through her nonprofit, The Cure Starts Now.

A large fire broke out at the General Electric Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky, on Friday morning, with no reported injuries. The blaze, which had gone to at least four alarms, sent thick smoke into the air as firefighters worked to contain the damage. The cause of the fire is currently unknown.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif received a hero's welcome in Tehran after nuclear talks with US Secretary of State John Kerry. Zarif, 54-56, has a background in international relations and spent time in the US, where he earned degrees and had children. He has played a key role in Iran's re-entry into the international community and will continue talks with Kerry to finalize a nuclear agreement.

A Connecticut judge has denied a motion to allow a 17-year-old girl with Hodgkin lymphoma to return home after completing chemotherapy, citing concerns she is a flight risk. The teen, Cassandra C., has been in temporary state custody since December and has undergone forced chemo treatments. Her attorneys plan to appeal the decision.

Researchers claim that "Double Falsehood," a play published in 1728, was actually written by William Shakespeare with the help of John Fletcher. Using computer software to analyze writing styles, the scholars found a strong match between the play and Shakespeare's works. The findings suggest that Shakespeare may have written the play more than a century before its publication.

French prosecutor Brice Robin says he is not aware of any video footage from Germanwings Flight 9525, contradicting claims by two magazines that they have seen a cell phone video of the plane's final moments. The magazines, Bild and Paris Match, described the video as showing passengers screaming and cries of "My God" in several languages. Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had battled depression and had a valid medical certificate, Lufthansa said.

US citizen Emy Afalava, a decorated veteran born in American Samoa, is suing for the right to vote, arguing that the Constitution's 14th Amendment guarantees citizenship to all people born in US territories. Despite being subject to US law, Afalava and other American Samoans are denied citizenship rights. A federal court decision on the case could come soon.

Blue Bell Creameries has temporarily shut down a manufacturing plant in Oklahoma after listeria contamination was found in a serving of ice cream. The CDC warned consumers not to eat certain products made at the plant, which has been linked to a listeria outbreak in Kansas. The recall affects certain 3-ounce servings and institutional products, but not all Blue Bell ice cream products.

Al-Shabaab claimed responsibility for an attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya, killing and taking hostages. The attack is part of a deteriorating security situation in East Africa, with Al-Shabaab having carried out a string of recent attacks in Kenya. The group's activities are driven by radical ideology and fueled by regional instability and socioeconomic challenges.

US protests to Russia after a fighter jet intercepts a US reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in an "unsafe and unprofessional manner". The incident involved a Russian SU-27 and a US RC-135U, with the US saying the Russian jet performed aggressive maneuvers. The US will file a formal complaint through diplomatic channels.

A hooded angel with black wings, created by artist Phillip Hyman, has become an icon of the Black Lives Matter movement after appearing near the site where Walter Scott was shot and killed by a police officer in North Charleston, South Carolina. The artwork, which Hyman created as a way to mourn with Scott's family, has been used in protests and has taken on a life of its own. Hyman says he is letting the artwork "do what it's supposed to do" as a symbol of the movement.

North Charleston police officer Michael Slager, fired and charged with murder, shot and killed unarmed black man Walter Scott. Bystander video shows discrepancies in initial police reports, contradicting Slager's claim that Scott tried to take his Taser. Scott was shot 8 times, 5 times hitting him, as he fled from Slager.

ISIS claims to have launched an assault on Iraq's largest oil refinery, the Baiji refinery, and controls parts of the facility. Iraqi government officials deny the claim, saying they remain in full control. The refinery's status is unclear, but it is a key strategic target.

Nashville's district attorney has banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals after the practice was revealed to have been used four times in the past five years. The use of sterilization as a punishment has sparked controversy, with some drawing comparisons to the eugenics movement. The constitutionality of sterilization as a punishment is unclear, but it may be permissible if chosen voluntarily as part of a plea deal.

More than 25,000 people have contracted Ebola in the past year, with over 10,000 fatalities. While the number of new cases has dropped, dozens are still infected weekly and concerns remain about unknown transmission chains. The outbreak has exposed flaws in government systems and highlighted the ongoing risk of new infections.

The NCAA has claimed it has no legal responsibility to ensure the academic integrity of courses offered to student-athletes at its member institutions. The claim was made in response to a lawsuit filed by former University of North Carolina athletes who alleged they did not receive a real education due to an academic fraud scandal. The NCAA's stance has been criticized as contradictory to its public statements about prioritizing the education of student-athletes.

An explosion at a chemical plant in China's Fujian province injured six people and sparked a huge fire. The blast occurred at an oil storage facility after a leak, and over 600 firefighters were deployed to battle the blaze. The plant produces paraxylene, a chemical used in polyester production, and has been the subject of past protests and a previous explosion in 2013.

The author of this opinion piece is calling for police body cameras after the fatal shooting of Walter Scott by Officer Michael Slager, citing the video evidence as proof that the officer's actions were unjustified. The author argues that body cameras could have prevented the tragedy and could help break a cycle of destruction between law enforcement and minority communities. Widespread use of body cameras could also help address racial bias in policing, the author says.

Tensions are running high at the VII Summit of the Americas in Panama City, where US President Barack Obama's meeting with Cuba's Raul Castro is being overshadowed by Venezuela's President Nicolas Maduro's accusations of a US plot to overthrow him. Maduro has rallied support from other Latin American leaders, including Cuba, after the US imposed sanctions on Venezuelan officials for human rights abuses. The developments have turned the summit into a "triangle of tension" between the US, Cuba, and Venezuela.

A nuclear submarine under repair at a Russian shipyard caught fire during welding work. The fire is burning insulation between the submarine's hulls, but there is no ammunition on board and no one was injured. The nuclear fuel had been unloaded from the submarine's reactor and the fire poses no threat, a shipyard spokesman said.

Tropical storm Maysak, also known as Chedeng, is approaching the Philippines, bringing winds of over 70 mph and flash flood warnings. Authorities have taken precautions, including evacuations and bans on outdoor activities, ahead of expected landfall Sunday. The storm is forecast to pass through the southeastern coast of Isabela province and exit the country by Monday.

NFL legend Deion Sanders publicly called out his son, Deion Sanders Jr., on Twitter for claiming he only eats "hood doughnuts." The elder Sanders reminded his son that he has a trust fund and other privileges, telling him to "stop the hood stuff." The exchange played out on Twitter, with the younger Sanders seemingly taking the criticism in stride.

Guatemala struggles with epidemic levels of gender-based violence, with nearly 10 out of every 100,000 women killed, and many more cases of violence and abuse going unreported. The country's weak judicial system and deeply entrenched culture of machismo and impunity contribute to the problem. Efforts by local organizations and international groups aim to address the issue, but more action is needed.

Indian police require cattle owners in Malegaon to photograph and identify their cows amid a state-wide ban on beef sales and consumption. The move aims to prevent cow slaughter, a non-bailable offense in Maharashtra state, where cows are considered holy. Over 100 owners have complied with the order, as police seek to create a database to track cattle.

Indian police are deploying pepper-spraying drones to control violent protests and unruly crowds. The drones, equipped with cameras and pepper spray, will be used in Lucknow and have sparked concerns about suppression of free speech. The move has received mixed reactions, with some calling for regulation and dialogue instead of force.

Don McLean's handwritten manuscript of "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's. The song, released in 1971, is a cultural anthem that has become a timeless classic, known for its hybrid of modern poetry and folk ballad. McLean's song has been ranked as one of the greatest songs of the 20th century by the Recording Industry of America and the National Endowment of the Arts.

London's Hatton Garden vault was raided over Easter, with thieves using a method not seen in the city for over 40 years, cracking open dozens of safety deposit boxes. The heist, likened to a scene from "Ocean 11", is believed to have been carried out by a sophisticated gang with inside information. Police are investigating, looking for forensic evidence and interviewing witnesses to track down the thieves.

7-Eleven is hosting a Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day on Saturday, allowing customers to fill their own containers for $1.49. Cups must be sanitary and fit through a 10-inch hole on in-store displays. The promotion kicks off peak Slurpee season.

Rand Paul, who declared his presidential candidacy, faces criticism from a former Kentucky state senator who questions his commitment to civil rights and voting rights. The critic argues that Paul's record shows he is out of touch with minority communities and trying to "take our country back" to a previous era. The senator says Paul's views are outdated and disqualify him from leading the country.

A Lamborghini crashed into a guardrail at Walt Disney World Speedway on Sunday, killing one passenger and injuring the driver. The driver, 24-year-old Tavon Watson, lost control of the vehicle during the Exotic Driving Experience. The passenger, 36-year-old Gary Terry, died at the scene.

Aaron Hernandez's defense team rested its case on Monday, after presenting fewer than a dozen witnesses, in contrast to the prosecution's 131. The jury will now consider evidence including testimony from Hernandez's fiancée and his former NFL boss, as well as disputed forensic analysis of shoeprints and video footage. Closing arguments are set for Tuesday, paving the way for jury deliberations.

Chinese authorities have detained five women's rights activists for "creating disturbances" ahead of International Women's Day, sparking concerns about the government's commitment to reform. The activists, who have used innovative tactics to raise awareness about gender inequality, face a legal deadline of April 13 for release or formal arrest. Their detention has raised concerns about China's treatment of independent activists and its progress on women's rights.

Former Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley says Hillary Clinton's status as Democratic frontrunner is not inevitable, citing examples of underdog candidates who have succeeded. O'Malley, a potential presidential contender, is making the rounds in Iowa, where Clinton leads in polls by over 40 points. Clinton is set to officially launch her campaign on Sunday.

The mother of Odin Lloyd, a 27-year-old man killed in 2013, spoke emotionally in court about her son's life and legacy after Aaron Hernandez was convicted and sentenced to life in prison for his murder. Odin Lloyd was described by family members as a champion of family, a gifted athlete, and a hard worker with a sense of humor. Hernandez was sentenced to life in prison for the first-degree murder of Lloyd.

Ted Cruz is courting evangelical voters in Iowa, a crucial state in the Republican presidential nomination process, by showcasing his faith and championing social issues. The Texas senator is counting on support from the Christian right to propel him forward in a crowded GOP field. Cruz's campaign is banking on a strong showing in Iowa to boost his national profile.

Marvel and X-Men franchises unveiled new character images ahead of upcoming releases. Paul Bettany debuted as the Vision in a poster for "Avengers: Age of Ultron", while Ben Hardy was revealed as Angel in "X-Men: Apocalypse". Jamie Bell also showed off his CGI-enhanced look as The Thing in the "Fantastic Four" reboot.

Italian Coast Guard rescues 978 migrants in Mediterranean Sea, off Libya coast. Over 10,000 migrants have arrived in Italy this year, with 480 deaths reported since January. Many migrants flee violence, trafficking, and persecution in Africa and Middle East.

French-language TV network TV5Monde was hit by a cyberattack, crippling its broadcasts and social media accounts. The network regained control of one of its 11 channels and its Facebook page Thursday. ISIS logos appeared on TV5Monde social media accounts, but there was no claim of responsibility.

David Lynch will no longer direct the revival of "Twin Peaks" due to a disagreement over financing. Lynch announced his departure via Twitter, saying the network wasn't offering enough money to produce the show as he envisioned. Showtime, which will air the series, expressed disappointment at Lynch's decision.

High-profile trials conclude in Massachusetts as Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev face juries. Meanwhile, Sen. Rand Paul officially announces his presidential bid and Chicago holds a mayoral runoff election between Rahm Emanuel and Jesus "Chuy" Garcia. Ferguson, Missouri, also holds elections in the wake of Michael Brown's death.

Tornadoes reported in Kansas, with multiple sightings near Wichita and in southwestern Kansas. A tornado may have also touched down in Missouri, causing wind damage and flooding. More storms are forecast for the Midwest and Mississippi River Valley on Thursday.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison for the 2008 murder of her ex-boyfriend Travis Alexander. The sentence was handed down by Judge Sherry Stephens, who rejected the possibility of early release. Arias had expressed remorse for her actions before the sentencing.

A Delaware family of four was hospitalized after falling ill at a luxury villa in the US Virgin Islands, and the EPA found the presence of restricted pesticide methyl bromide at the villa. The EPA is investigating whether the family was exposed to the pesticide during a March 18 fumigation at the resort. The incident is also under criminal investigation by the US Department of Justice.

Rolling Stone magazine faces potential defamation lawsuits after a review found its article on a purported gang rape at University of Virginia was "deeply flawed". The magazine has apologized for damaging the reputation of Phi Kappa Psi fraternity and UVA administrators and students. Legal experts say a defamation case could be viable, but hurdles remain, including proving false statements were made with reckless disregard for the truth.

FBI agents and task force officers chased a suspect, Kevone Charleston, 36, through a Georgia neighborhood, exchanging gunfire and crashing several vehicles. Two agents were injured when their SUV flipped over. Charleston was shot and taken into custody, ending a string of 32 suspected commercial robberies.

Alaska Airlines Flight 448 made an emergency landing in Seattle after a ramp agent was discovered sleeping in the cargo hold and made noise by banging on the plane. The agent, who had apparently fallen asleep, was unharmed and the plane landed safely with all 176 passengers and crew. The incident is under investigation by Alaska Airlines.

A US judge has ruled that Craig Hicks, charged with killing three Muslim college students in North Carolina, can face the death penalty. Hicks, 46, is accused of shooting Yusor Mohammad, Deah Barakat, and Razan Abu-Salha in the head in a killing that authorities are investigating as a possible hate crime. He faces three counts of first-degree murder.

Afghanistan's women's rights activists face increasing attacks and threats from the Taliban, tribal warlords, and government officials, Amnesty International reported. The group's report calls for authorities to address the issue, citing a 20% increase in women killed in 2013. Activists say they often receive little support from authorities and face significant risks in their work.

A New York judge has authorized serving divorce papers on a husband via Facebook, marking a new frontier in the law of "service of process". The method is being used as an alternative to traditional in-person service, which can be difficult when defendants are evasive or hard to find. Online service is seen as a more reliable option than methods like "nail and mail" service or publication in obscure newspapers.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, founder of the "Hour of Power" television ministry and Crystal Cathedral megachurch, has died at 88. Schuller, a televangelist and proponent of "possibility thinking," reached millions with his upbeat message before his family's ministry faced financial and succession troubles. He died Thursday after a battle with esophageal cancer.

Four workers died and 45 were injured in a massive fire on an oil rig off Mexico's coast. The fire was extinguished by nightfall after a multi-hour battle involving at least 10 boats. Pemex said there was no oil spill and the platform did not collapse.

Kansas Governor Sam Brownback has signed a law banning a common second-term abortion procedure, known as "dismemberment abortion". The law, the first of its kind in the US, restricts the dilation and evacuation procedure, with exceptions to protect the life or health of the mother. The move has been hailed by anti-abortion groups and criticized by reproductive rights advocates.

Chinese TV host Bi Fujian apologized for cursing late Chairman Mao Zedong at a dinner party, saying his comments had "grave social consequences". Bi's improvised lyrics were caught on camera and sparked controversy, with some calling for him to be punished. His employer, state-run CCTV, said it would investigate the incident.

University of Kentucky basketball player Andrew Harrison apologized for using a racial slur to refer to Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky after Saturday's game. Harrison, who is black, said his words were "in jest" and meant no disrespect, and Kaminsky said he has forgiven him. Harrison reached out to Kaminsky to apologize and wished him good luck in Monday's national title game.

Arrested Development to return for fifth season with 17 episodes. Executive producer Brian Grazer says the new season is coming, though Netflix has no comment. Casting for the new season has not been announced.

The Large Hadron Collider, the world's largest particle accelerator, has restarted after a two-year shutdown, with scientists completing final tests and circulating the first beams of particles. The $3.3 billion machine aims to recreate the conditions of the Big Bang and uncover secrets of the universe, including the origin of mass and dark matter. The LHC will collide particles at near-light speed, generating vast amounts of data to help scientists better understand the universe.

An Iranian military observation aircraft flew within 50 yards of a US Navy helicopter in the Persian Gulf, sparking concern that local Iranian forces may not be fully under control. The incident, which was deemed "unsafe" by US military officials, occurred despite recent professional interactions between Iranian and US forces. The US is considering a diplomatic protest over the incident.

A US jury found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all 30 counts related to the Boston Marathon bombing. The trial will now move to a penalty phase to determine if Tsarnaev, 21, will face the death penalty. The jury will weigh aggravating and mitigating factors, including his youth and mental health history, to decide his fate.

Indian police arrested four employees of ethnic-wear chain FabIndia after a minister discovered a security camera overlooking a changing room in one of its stores. The camera was found to be able to take photos of customers, and the employees face charges of voyeurism and breach of privacy. The store's manager and company officials are also under scrutiny.

Iran plans to lift ban on women attending some sports events. Deputy Sports Minister says "women and families" will be allowed into stadiums for certain events in the next year. Details on which events will be open to women are unclear.

Indian software pioneer Ramalinga Raju and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their roles in a $1.6 billion corporate fraud case. Raju, former chairman of Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000. The scandal has been compared to the Enron Corp. scandal and is considered India's biggest corporate scandal in memory.

A woman with cancer was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight from Hawaii to California because she didn't have a doctor's note to fly. The airline apologized and said it was acting out of concern for her well-being, but acknowledged the situation was handled poorly. The incident caused disruptions, including causing the woman to miss her chemotherapy appointment.

Turkish singer-songwriter Kayahan Acar died of cancer at 66 in Istanbul. He was a beloved musician known for his love songs and had performed in the Eurovision Song Contest in 1990. Kayahan had battled cancer several times since his initial diagnosis in 1990.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized the Iran nuclear deal, saying it doesn't roll back Iran's nuclear program and allows the country to keep a vast infrastructure in place. Netanyahu's comments drew pushback from Democrats, with Sen. Dianne Feinstein saying he needs to "contain himself." The deal has sparked partisan sparring, with Republicans saying it gives Iran too much flexibility and Democrats defending it as a better alternative to war.

Multiple shootings occurred in the Washington, D.C. area late Thursday, including one at the US Census Bureau headquarters and another in a popular restaurant area. Authorities say the incidents were connected and began with a domestic kidnapping. A suspect was involved in a shootout with police and was wounded, along with a police officer.

Chelsea Manning, serving 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents, has joined Twitter, posting messages via a third-party firm. She will use a voice phone to dictate tweets, which will be posted on her behalf, as she is not allowed internet access in prison. Manning has nearly 26,000 followers and plans to engage in two-way conversations on the platform.
Rapper Nelly arrested in Tennessee on drug charges. Authorities found methamphetamine, marijuana, and handguns on bus. Nelly, 40, posted bond and was released from jail.

A Delaware father is in stable condition after falling ill with his two teenage sons, possibly due to pesticide exposure, while on a trip to the US Virgin Islands. The family's mother, Theresa Devine, was treated and released, while the sons remain in critical condition. The EPA found evidence of methyl bromide, a restricted pesticide, at the family's rental villa.

Governments in Asia are increasingly using laws and violence to silence online critics and journalists, with many facing imprisonment, financial penalties, and even death. Online journalists and bloggers are becoming the most vulnerable targets, with countries such as China, Vietnam, and Bangladesh leading the way in suppressing online dissent. In Bangladesh, at least two bloggers have been hacked to death in recent weeks, highlighting the growing threat to online journalists.

Nina Dobrev to leave "The Vampire Diaries" at end of season. Fans express disappointment and anger over her departure, fearing the show's quality will suffer. Dobrev's exit comes after six seasons on the show.

Syrian government forces and anti-regime groups, including ISIS, have intensified fighting in the Yarmouk refugee camp near Damascus, causing widespread destruction and civilian casualties. The camp, home to thousands of Palestinians, has been besieged for years, with residents facing dire shortages of food, water, and medical care. Only 18,000 of the camp's original 100,000 residents remain, according to the UN.

NASA scientists discuss prospects for discovering life elsewhere in the universe over the next decade. Nearly 2,000 exoplanets have been discovered, and astronomers estimate 40 billion Earth-like planets may exist in the Milky Way galaxy. Signs of life on exoplanets may be discovered in coming decades, but communicating with intelligent life may be unlikely.

Massachusetts man Carlos Colina, 32, faces murder charges after human remains were found in a duffel bag in Cambridge. The remains have been identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, who knew Colina. Colina is also facing charges in another case involving alleged assault and battery.

Kanye West has settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzi photographer Daniel Ramos, who he assaulted at Los Angeles International Airport in 2013. The terms of the settlement were not disclosed, but Ramos' lawyer said West apologized to her client. The incident had been caught on video and West had previously pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor count of battery.

US President Barack Obama's desire for a nuclear deal with Iran has led to a weak agreement that favours Iran, critics say. The deal allows Iran to keep much of its nuclear infrastructure and does not require it to dismantle its facilities. The agreement has sparked concerns among US allies in the Middle East, who fear it will embolden Iran.

Police officer Michael Slager was arrested and charged with murder after a video showed him killing unarmed black man Walter Scott during a traffic stop. The incident highlights the need for comprehensive data on police killings, which is mandated by a 1994 law but has never been fully implemented. The lack of data makes it difficult to determine the scope of the problem and whether certain factors contribute to excessive force by police.

Five Americans who were monitored for Ebola exposure at a Nebraska hospital have been released. The clinicians, who worked in Sierra Leone, were exposed to a colleague with Ebola but did not develop the disease. All 17 patients being monitored are expected to be released by Thursday.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars has reached a 13th week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, the longest-leading song of the 2010s. The song is one of only 10 to spend at least 13 weeks at No. 1 in the chart's history. Natalie La Rose's "Somebody" featuring Jeremih debuts in the top 10 at No. 10.

Fans of movies like "Lost", "Empire Records", "Titanic", "Miss Congeniality", "Mean Girls", and "Back to the Future Part II" celebrated their own unofficial holidays on April 8, April 14, April 25, October 3, and October 21. These dates were made famous by their appearances in the films. The observances were marked on social media, with fans paying homage to their favorite movies.

Lifetime has acquired the rights to "Grace of Monaco," a biographical drama starring Nicole Kidman as Princess Grace Kelly, for a Memorial Day premiere. The film, which was shown at Cannes last year, was initially expected to be a theatrical release but underperformed in international markets. The Weinstein Co. will sell the film to Lifetime for a reported $3 million.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward has passed an ordinance to recognize same-sex partnerships, allowing couples to receive some rights such as hospital visitation and co-signing tenancy agreements. The move is seen as a step towards marriage equality in socially conservative Japan, although a national law is still needed to achieve full equality. The decision may inspire other municipalities to follow suit.

California's drought is expected to impact food prices nationwide, with fresh fruit and vegetable prices projected to rise 2.5-3.5% and 2-3% respectively. The drought, now in its fourth year, has already led to price increases for certain produce, including berries, broccoli, and grapes. The effects of the drought may be mitigated by a strong US dollar and lower oil prices.

The University of Michigan will screen "American Sniper" despite objections from some students who objected to its depiction of the Iraq War. A petition with over 200 signatures had called for the movie to be pulled, citing concerns it reflected negatively on the Middle East. A counter-petition led to the university reversing its decision.

The 2015 MTV Movie Awards featured a mix of hits and misses, with Amy Schumer's opening segment and monologue receiving praise, while moments like an archery fail and a Shailene Woodley speech went awry. Channing Tatum's twerk for Jennifer Lopez and a performance by Fall Out Boy and Fetty Wap were among the highlights. The ceremony's jokes and performances were often hit-or-miss, with some, like a "Gone Girl" joke, falling flat.

A debris fragment from a Japanese boat, likely from the 2011 earthquake and tsunami, has washed up off the Oregon coast. The boat fragment contained several yellowtail jack fish, native to Japanese waters, which will be taken to the Oregon Coast Aquarium. The debris will be disposed of in a landfill.

Nigeria marked the one-year anniversary of the kidnapping of 276 schoolgirls by Boko Haram, with President-elect Muhammadu Buhari vowing to combat the group. The girls, aged 16-18, were abducted from a school in Chibok and have not been seen since, sparking global outrage and a #BringBackOurGirls campaign. Despite promises to rescue them, the girls remain missing, and Boko Haram continues to control parts of northeastern Nigeria.

Easter, a pivotal holiday in the Christian calendar, is often misunderstood even among Christians. The Easter Triduum, comprising Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Sunday, represents a spiritual progression from darkness to light, mirroring the human experience of suffering, transition, and transformation. This three-day sequence, observed annually, offers a profound exploration of the human condition and the promise of renewal.

Kenyan authorities have frozen 86 bank accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters in the wake of a university massacre that killed 147 people. The move is part of a crackdown on terror financing following the attack, which the militant group claimed responsibility for. The Kenyan government has also launched airstrikes targeting Al-Shabaab training camps in Somalia.

Jia Jiang, a Chinese-born American, quit his six-figure job to follow his entrepreneurial dreams, and in response to his own fear of rejection, embarked on a project where he subjected himself to 100 days of rejection. His blog and subsequent book, "Rejection Proof," aim to help others overcome their fear of rejection and turn it into opportunity. Jiang shares eight tips for making rejection work for you, including reframing rejection as a numbers game and not taking it personally.

US Attorney General Eric Holder has reminded Justice Department employees, including FBI and DEA agents, that soliciting prostitution is prohibited and can result in suspension or firing. The memo comes amid reports of agents misbehaving with prostitutes while on duty overseas. The directive applies to all times, including off-duty and personal leave.

A Wayne Community College employee was shot and killed by a former work-study program participant on Monday. The suspect, Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, was arrested in Florida after fleeing the scene and may have committed a hate crime. Authorities are investigating possible ties to a white supremacist gang.

Amnesty International reports that the use of the death penalty remained a concern globally in 2014, with 607 executions recorded worldwide, down from 778 in 2013. Several countries, including Pakistan, Iran, and Iraq, resumed or increased executions, often in response to terrorism or crime. Despite this, the trend is towards abolition, with 140 countries now abolitionist in law or practice.

Duke University student admits to hanging a noose from a tree near a student union, prompting an investigation and student conduct review. The student, whose identity was not disclosed, is no longer on campus. The incident is one of several recent racist events to affect college students nationwide.

Richard Dysart, the Emmy-winning actor known for his role as Leland McKenzie in the NBC drama "L.A. Law," has died at 86. Dysart appeared in over 200 films and TV shows, including "The Thing," "Being There," and "Wall Street." He died Sunday at his home in Santa Monica after a long illness.

Easter, a cornerstone of the Christian faith, is celebrated on a Sunday that falls between March 22 and April 25, with the date determined by lunar and solar cycles. The holiday's timing is tied to Passover and the vernal equinox, resulting in Eastern Orthodox Christians often celebrating on a different date than Western Christians. The traditions surrounding Easter, including the Easter bunny and eggs, have evolved over time and vary across cultures.

Comedian Chris Rock sparked debate on Twitter by documenting a traffic stop, posting a photo of himself behind the wheel with police lights in the background. The incident is the latest in a series of stops he has experienced, highlighting racial disparities in police treatment. Rock's tweets drew both support and criticism, with some accusing him of race-baiting and others praising him for bringing attention to the issue.

Lynyrd Skynyrd's original drummer, Robert Lewis Burns Jr., 64, died in a car crash in Georgia on Friday night. Burns was not restrained at the time of the crash, which occurred shortly before midnight. He was part of the band's original lineup from 1965 to 1975.

A viral photo of a cat on stairs is sparking debate over whether the cat is going up or down. The image, posted on Imgur and shared on 9gag.com, has become a social media sensation. Advertisers are already capitalizing on the meme.

US and its allies reach framework agreement with Iran limiting Tehran's nuclear program, effectively blocking development of a nuclear weapon. The deal reduces Iran's uranium stockpile, cuts centrifuges, and implements inspections; it does not require total elimination of Iran's nuclear program. Critics' assertions that the deal has flaws and sunsets are disputed by experts.

University of Virginia faces ongoing scrutiny over its handling of sexual assault cases, having never expelled a student for the crime despite numerous allegations. An investigation by the Virginia attorney general and a US Department of Education probe are underway. The retraction of a disputed Rolling Stone article has sparked concerns that it may set back efforts to address campus rape.

Indiana Pacers player Chris Copeland was stabbed in New York City early Wednesday after a dispute with a 22-year-old man. Two Atlanta Hawks players, Pero Antic and Thabo Sefolosha, were arrested on charges of obstruction and disorderly conduct after they interfered with the police investigation. Copeland is in stable condition with a knife wound to his elbow and abdomen.

Twisted Sister will embark on a farewell tour in 2016, titled "Forty and F*ck It," to celebrate its 40th anniversary. The tour will feature new drummer Mike Portnoy and two special shows in honor of late drummer A.J. Pero. The band's final tour will mark the end of its 40-year run.

John Travolta, a prominent Scientologist, dismissed HBO's documentary "Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief" as negative and not worth commenting on. Travolta, who credits Scientology with helping him cope with his son's death, said he has had a positive experience with the Church and won't speak out against it. The documentary, based on a book by Lawrence Wright, is critical of Scientology.

The film "Furious 7" earned a record $146 million over the weekend, with many moviegoers saying the final scenes, which paid tribute to late star Paul Walker, were emotionally moving. The film's makers used body doubles, computer-generated images, and Walker's brothers to complete his scenes, and chose to retire his character rather than kill him off. The movie's ending, which showed Walker as having retired to family life, was widely praised as a fitting tribute.

The fifth season of "Game of Thrones" premieres Sunday, with major story arcs set to converge as the show passes its halfway point. Expect battles to intensify and drama to escalate as characters like Arya, Sansa, and Cersei take center stage. The season will also deviate from George RR Martin's books, with some plotlines moving ahead of the source material.

Several people have survived incredible ordeals at sea, including being stranded for weeks or months with limited resources. Louis Jordan was rescued 200 miles off the North Carolina coast after his sailboat capsized, while Jose Salvador Alvarenga survived 13 months adrift in the Pacific. Others, including Ron Ingraham, Adrian Vasquez, and Hiromitsu Shinkawa, also survived against-the-odds experiences at sea or during natural disasters.

The "Star Wars" saga is being released in digital HD, featuring the first six movies and exclusive behind-the-scenes content. The collection includes a focus on sound effects, including the insect-like sounds of the Geonosians. The release marks the first time the films have been available for digital download.

Boston Marathon bombing suspect Dzhokhar Tsarnaev found guilty on all 30 counts. Victims and their families react with mixed emotions, saying justice has been served but can never fully make up for the pain. The guilty verdict brings closure, but survivors say their lives will never be the same.

China's former security czar, Zhou Yongkang, has been formally charged with accepting bribes, abusing power, and leaking state secrets. Zhou, a former member of the Communist Party's top decision-making body, is the highest-ranking official to face corruption charges. His case will be tried in Tianjin, a city near Beijing.

A 21-year-old quadriplegic with cerebral palsy was abandoned in a Philadelphia park for over 4 days with minimal supplies. The suspect is his mother, who allegedly left him there to visit her boyfriend in Maryland. She faces charges including aggravated assault, neglect, and kidnapping.

Walmart has emerged as a prominent voice opposing "religious freedom" laws that critics say discriminate against gays and lesbians, with the company's opposition helping to galvanize a broader backlash against such measures. The company's stance reflects shifting public opinion and growing support for gay rights, with some prominent Republicans urging the party to take notice. Walmart's actions have put it at odds with some in the Republican Party, which the company's PAC has traditionally supported.

Pope Francis has reawakened the faith of a lapsed Catholic, who had become disillusioned with the Church's rules and judgmental attitude. The Pope's message of love, acceptance, and non-judgment has resonated with the individual, who feels welcomed back into the Church. Cardinal Gerald Lacroix, one of the Pope's newly appointed cardinals, attributes the Pope's approach to his deep spirituality and commitment to living the Gospel.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau, who served prison time for her affair with a 13-year-old student, and her husband Vili Fualaau are marking their 10th wedding anniversary. The couple, who have two teen daughters, are set to appear in an ABC interview, discussing their relationship and her plans to teach again. Letourneau Fualaau is a registered sex offender.

Hillary Clinton has officially announced her candidacy for the 2016 US presidential election, making her a symbol of gender equality in the process. Her campaign's outcome will be scrutinized for its implications for women in politics, regardless of whether she wins or loses. Clinton's experience will be seen as a test of whether the US is ready to elect a woman to the White House.

Amnesty International's annual report on the death penalty says governments are using the threat of terrorism to justify executions, despite a 22% global decline in executions in 2014. At least 607 people were executed worldwide, with China, Iran, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia among the top executioners. The report notes a spike in death sentences, with 2,466 people sentenced to death in 2014, a 28% increase from 2013.

Japan's Defense Minister Gen Nakatani says the country's Air Self Defense Force has never encountered a UFO. The response came to a query from lawmaker Antonio Inoki, who asked about the military's preparedness for extraterrestrial threats. Nakatani said jets are scrambled to investigate unidentified flying objects, but none have been confirmed to be of extraterrestrial origin.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce a film about the Boston Marathon bombing, titled "Patriots' Day", which will be told from the perspective of Boston Police Commissioner Ed Davis. The film will draw on research and footage from CBS News' "60 Minutes". This is the second film announced about the bombing, following Fox's "Boston Strong".

Democrats Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb, both considering presidential runs, appeared together at a Polk County Democrats event in Iowa, showcasing their differing styles. O'Malley, a former Maryland governor, was energetic and interactive, while Webb, a former Virginia senator and Vietnam War veteran, was more subdued. Both trail far behind frontrunner Hillary Clinton in polls.

Nine British citizens, including four children, were arrested at the Turkey-Syria border while attempting to cross into Syria illegally. The group, consisting of three men and two women, all held British passports. The incident has prompted the UK Foreign Office to seek information from Turkish authorities.

US Department of Justice charges FedEx with 15 counts including conspiracy, money laundering, and violating the Controlled Substances Act, alleging the company knowingly shipped prescription drugs from illegal pharmacies. FedEx denies the charges, arguing it is a "common carrier" exempt from possession charges. The case raises questions about corporate liability and the limits of prosecution.

Kenyan citizens mourned the 147 victims of last week's terrorist attack at Garissa University College, sharing their stories and photos on social media. The attack, claimed by Al-Shabaab, was one of the deadliest in Kenya's history, killing mostly students. Kenyans marked Easter Sunday with somber church services.

Sweden offers 480 days of parental leave, with 390 days paid at 80% of income, to encourage shared parenting. Fathers must take 60 of those days, or "daddy months," or they are lost. Despite the policy, only 12% of Swedish couples share the leave equally.

US President Barack Obama said he is committed to ensuring Israel maintains a military advantage over Iran. Obama's comments come amid criticism from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the nuclear deal with Iran. Obama said the US would stand by Israel if it were attacked by any state.

US religious freedom laws spark controversy; 20 states have enacted laws similar to Indiana's Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which critics say can be used to discriminate against gays. Several court cases have tested the laws, with some religious minorities winning protections, such as a Native American's right to possess eagle feathers and a Brazilian faith's use of a sacramental tea.

Five Chinese feminists detained for planning International Women's Day events may face up to five years in prison on charges of "assembling a crowd to disturb public order." The women, who were detained on March 6-7, were campaigning for gender equality and against sexual harassment. A decision on formal charges is expected by Monday.

Selena, the late Tejano star, is being brought back in a new way with a hologram-like figure called "Selena the One." The technology will allow the digital embodiment to walk, talk, sing, and dance, and will be used to release new music and collaborate with current artists. The project is expected to launch in 2018, with a crowdfunding campaign starting April 16.

Minnesota Rep. Michele Bachmann compared President Obama to the co-pilot of Germanwings Flight 9525, saying he is "flying his entire nation into the rocks" with his Iran deal. The comment sparked widespread criticism on her Facebook page. Bachmann has been a vocal critic of Obama's Iran policy, previously urging him to "bomb Iran".

Ryan Gosling's directorial debut "Lost River" has sparked controversy, but its portrayal of a decaying Detroit has been widely praised. Gosling cited his affection for the city and its history as the inspiration for the film, which began as a collection of speculative shots of the Brewster-Douglass Projects. The movie's release comes as Detroit faces bankruptcy and urban renewal efforts.

UK police charged a 19-year-old man, Yahya Rashid, with terror offenses after he was arrested at Luton airport on his return from Turkey. Rashid faces charges of preparing acts of terrorism and assisting others to commit acts of terrorism. He is due to appear in court on Wednesday.

Mötley Crüe's Vince Neil butchered the US national anthem before a Las Vegas football game, sparking a renewed debate about renditions of "The Star-Spangled Banner". Several celebrities, including Whitney Houston, Jimi Hendrix, and Michael Bolton, have had their own infamous performances of the anthem. Some have been praised, while others have been widely criticized.

Hundreds of World War I soldiers' graffiti have been discovered in an underground city in France, dating back nearly 100 years. The inscriptions, found on walls near Naours, France, include names, units, and hometowns of soldiers from Australia, Britain, and the US. Over 1,800 names have been identified so far, with many more still to be traced.

The Palestinian Authority has officially become the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court, giving the court jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories. The move was opposed by Israel and the US, which do not recognize Palestine as a state. The ICC will now begin a preliminary examination of alleged war crimes committed in Palestinian territories since June 2014.

Anthony Ray Hinton, 58, was released from Alabama's death row after nearly 30 years, following the dismissal of charges in a 1985 murder case. Hinton, who maintained his innocence, was cleared after firearms experts found that the revolver linked to the crimes could not be matched to evidence. His lawyers and advocates cited the case as an example of the need for reform in the US capital punishment system.

US taxpayers are set to receive an average refund of $3,000, making Tax Day a happy occasion for many. The tax filing process has become simpler, with many able to file for free online. Despite criticisms of the US tax system as complex and unfair, the refund checks are providing a welcome boost to many Americans.

Jordan Spieth maintained his lead at the Masters with a steady third round, despite a late double bogey. Spieth leads by four strokes heading into the final round. Tiger Woods and others made big moves, but couldn't close the gap.

Liana Barrientos, 39, has been charged with two counts of offering a false instrument for filing after she lied on a 2010 marriage license application, claiming it was her first marriage. Barrientos has been married 10 times, mostly in a short period between 1999 and 2002, and is believed to still be married to four men. Prosecutors say the marriages were part of an immigration scam to gain permanent residence status for some of her husbands.

Memories Pizza in Indiana faced backlash after saying it would not cater a same-sex wedding, sparking boycotts and harassment. However, the restaurant also received over $842,000 in donations and support from people who back its right to practice its faith. The controversy highlights the debate over Indiana's Religious Freedom Restoration Act.

Vijay Chokalingam, brother of actress Mindy Kaling, applied to medical school as a black man, claiming a false racial identity to improve his chances of admission. He received only one acceptance, to a lower-ranked school, and experienced racism firsthand while pretending to be black. Chokalingam's actions have sparked debate about affirmative action and racial identity.

Antarctica recorded a temperature of 63.5°F (15.5°C) on March 24, possibly the highest ever recorded on the continent. The temperature was recorded at Argentina's Esperanza Base on the Antarctica Peninsula. The World Meteorological Organization will verify the record after reviewing the measurement and surrounding data.

US officials say there is no set timeline for a potential Iraqi-led operation to retake Mosul from ISIS. The operation, which has been planned for months, will require significant time and resources. Iraqi forces have made progress against ISIS, including the recapture of Tikrit, but Mosul's larger population and strategic importance make it a more complex target.

Irish bookmaker Paddy Power deleted a tweet that sparked outrage, saying it was meant as a joke. The tweet compared Liverpool fans' history of beating Newcastle to police killings of unarmed African-American men. The company faced a backlash, with many condemning the tweet as insensitive.

Mother of quadriplegic man charged with attempted murder after leaving him in woods for days. Nyia Parler, 41, to face additional charges including aggravated assault and reckless endangerment. Parler remains in treatment and will be extradited to Philadelphia once complete.

US Ambassador Mark Lippert was stabbed in Seoul on March 5. Kim Ki-Jong, 55, has been charged with attempted murder, assaulting a foreign envoy, and business obstruction. Kim's trial is set to begin within 14 days.

Jill Dillard, daughter of reality TV stars Jim Bob and Michelle Duggar, has given birth to a son named Israel David. The 9-pound, 10-ounce baby was born Monday, over a week past his due date. Jill and husband Derick are the first of the "19 Kids and Counting" family to have a child.

Universal's "Furious 7" is poised for a massive opening weekend in North America, with projections of $135-138 million, and has already earned a record-breaking $60 million internationally. The film, the latest in the Fast and Furious franchise, is getting a wide release in 4,003 US theaters and over 10,500 screens globally. It is on track to become the biggest opening of 2015 and one of the largest three-day openings in US history.

US Secret Service supervisor accused of assaulting female employee. The supervisor, Xavier Morales, was placed on administrative leave and his security clearance suspended. The incident is under investigation and is the latest in a series of scandals for the Secret Service.

Hillary Clinton has announced her candidacy for the 2016 presidential election. Clinton, a strong candidate with extensive experience, faces challenges including doubts about her authenticity, connections with the Democratic base, and lingering questions about her husband and personal life. To succeed, she must present an exciting vision for the White House and overcome concerns about her trustworthiness and potential liabilities.

The US Department of Justice will begin negotiations with Ferguson, Missouri to restructure its police department, which has been accused of racial discrimination and a pattern of abuse. The negotiations come after a report detailed widespread problems, including racist emails and excessive force, and recommendations for reforms. The city is also undergoing changes, with a new city council and police chief, but activists are pushing for more fundamental changes to the town's government and policing structure.

A US couple's pet cat, Felix, went missing at New York's John F. Kennedy Airport after Etihad Airways allegedly lost him following a flight from Abu Dhabi. The airline is investigating and has launched a search for the 2-year-old cat, who was traveling in a damaged carrier. The incident has raised concerns about the safety and care of pets during air travel.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued after drifting at sea for 66 days on a sailboat that capsized in a storm. He survived on collected rainwater and caught fish that were attracted to his laundry. Jordan was found in surprisingly good condition by a container ship crew and is recovering in a Virginia hospital.
